title: Deployment Mode Convergence Workshop - Alder Ventures POC
summary: Discovery / scoping workshop focused on POC success criteria, sizing benchmarks, and decision factors for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Alder wants latency under 200ms p95 for interactive workflows, cost guardrails, SOC2 + SSO, and a 6-week pilot with clear acceptance tests. Agreed next steps: pricing sheet, runbook, and a small synthetic benchmark within 10 days.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
action_items: Maya Chen | Share two-tier pricing (hosted vs dedicated) + example cost model | 2026-03-10
Carlos Ortega | Provide benchmark runbook + sample JMeter script and inference config | 2026-03-12
Ethan Cole | Deliver sample workload CSV (5000 example prompts) and latency targets | 2026-03-09
Jared Mills | Confirm VPC peering constraints and KMS requirements for private POC | 2026-03-11
next_steps: Redwood to run a synthetic benchmark on 1k concurrent sessions using their hosted test harness (no customer data) — results by 2026-03-17
Alder to review pricing and confirm whether Dedicated reserved capacity is acceptable for month-1
Schedule technical deep dive with Alder infra team (VPC, routing, firewall) week of 2026-03-15
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Narang (Alder CTO), Ethan Cole (Head ML), Jared Mills (Infra)
Shared links: https://redwood.dev/poc-runbook (deck), https://redwood.dev/benchmarks/sample-config (bench config)

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. Quick round-robin intro please?
00:08 Priya (Alder): Priya here, CTO. We want to get alignment on the POC goals and see which deployment lane we should pick — hosted first or go straight to dedicated or private. Timeline is tight.
00:18 Ethan (Alder): Hi, Ethan — lead ML. We'll be integrating an assistant that handles support triage and short summaries, mostly 50-200 token replies, heavy prompt branching. Target p95 latency <200ms if possible.
00:30 Jared (Alder): Jared, infra. My main concerns are data residency, KMS and firewall rules. We may need V-P-C peering and HSM for keys.
00:40 Maya: Great. Quick context — Redwood supports three modes: hosted API for fast onboarding, Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) for predictable throughput and isolation, and Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated workloads. We'll walk through tradeoffs and, importantly, acceptance criteria for the POC.
01:02 Carlos (Redwood SE): Hi all, I'll focus on benchmarks and runbook. Before that, can you map out expected QPS and concurrency? That shapes batching and cache behavior.
01:14 Ethan: So our expected hourly throughput is spiky — peak during morning surge and support hours. Peak parallel conversations maybe 600 concurrent sessions, average token length 120, token generation per session about 150 tokens. Overall steady state maybe 150-200 QPS, burst up to 1k QPS for short periods.
01:36 Carlos: Okay that's helpful. Quick note: for those numbers, Dedicated with continuous GPU pools usually gives predictable latency; hosted can meet it but we'd need to tune batching and maybe increase concurrency slots. Also we'll look at prefix caching — K-V cash — to reduce repetition cost.
01:55 Priya: When you say hosted can meet it, is that with our data in the cloud or does hosted bring chi-- any compliance issues? We need SOC2 Type II, SSO via SAML, and logs retained 13 months.
02:10 Maya: We have SOC2 attestation. SAML SSO and RBAC exist on the console. Retention can be extended as an add-on. For private POC we can offer a private control plane and customer-managed KMS/HSM.
02:24 Jared: For KMS we need bring-your-own-key and HSM-backed keys. Is that supported on hosted?
02:30 Carlos: BYOK is available on Private deployments; for Dedicated we can integrate with customer KMS in some regions but HSM-backed BYOK on hosted is limited. We'll enumerate exact options in the runbook.
03:00 Ethan: Okay acceptance criteria we want to propose: (1) p95 inference latency <200ms for interactive flows on pilot load; (2) 99.5% successful replies (no infra errors) over a 72 hour window; (3) cost estimate for sustained 200 QPS and for 1k QPS bursts; (4) security checklist: SOC2 docs, SAML, KMS plan. Does that sound reasonable?
03:25 Maya: That aligns with what we usually see. We'll add a 5th: model quality parity — we want no more than 5% delta in retrieval+generation quality vs your local baseline prompts (we'll use an eval set you provide).
03:40 Ethan: We'll deliver eval set.
03:45 Priya: Timelinewise we want pilot results in 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
03:51 Maya: Yes — typical flow: week 1 onboarding + workload delivery, week 2 benchmarking and config tuning, weeks 3-4 can be extended pilot + soak, week 5 final tuning, week 6 acceptance and wrap. If Dedicated or Private provisioning is needed, add 1-2 weeks for infra prep.
04:12 Jared: What's the provisioning lead time for Dedicated?
04:15 Carlos: If we allocate from a shared pool it can be immediate; reserved capacity procurement typical 2-3 weeks for contract and dedicated GPU pools. Private on-prem is the longest — depends on networking approvals.
04:30 Ethan: For benchmarking, do you prefer synthetic or replay of production traces?
04:35 Carlos: Start synthetic to validate latency under controlled load, then do a sanitized replay with your CSV of prompts to validate quality and cost. We'll provide a sample runner (JMeter + simple client) and the config.
04:50 Maya: Also we'll propose two acceptance benchmark suites: 1) 2-hour p95 soak at 200 QPS; 2) 30-minute burst at 1k QPS to validate throttling/fallback. Both should be run against the chosen deployment mode.
05:12 Priya: Can hosted run the 1k QPS burst? We don't want to commit dedicated budget if hosted handles it well.
05:20 Carlos: Hosted can handle it but with variable latency — autoscaling can help but cost may spike. Dedicated gives predictable tail latency because of reserved GPUs and controlled batching. Private depends entirely on your infra sizing.
05:34 Jared: About networking — VPC peering implies opening ports and cross-account peering. We need a clear list of rules to share with security.
05:40 Maya: We'll produce a networking checklist. Carlos, can you note that?
05:42 Carlos: Noted — I'll include port lists, IP ranges, and sample peering templates.
05:48 Ethan: Model sizing — which model family would you recommend for our 150 token generations? We want a balance of cost and latency.
05:55 Carlos: Depends on quality bar. For deterministic responses and lower cost, a 13B quantized variant will likely meet the target with p95 in the 100-250ms range on Dedicated GPUs. If you need higher quality, we can try a 34B or the Redwood-curated mix, but expect longer tails. We'll include kernel selection, quant options in the runbook.
06:20 Priya: Any mention of caching — how much improvement can we expect?
06:24 Carlos: For repeated prefixes, K-V cache can cut token compute by 30-70% depending on reuse. Our prefix/K-V caching works better for multi-turn sessions with repeated context.
06:35 Ethan: For the private option, what's the standard telemetry footprint? We need traceability but not full request bodies to Redwood.
06:41 Maya: Private offers telemetry hooks with obfuscated payloads; we can send token-level cost, latencies, but you keep the raw text. We'll document exact telemetry fields.
06:55 Priya: Are there common gotchas you've seen in similar pilots?
07:00 Carlos: Yes — two things: first, underestimating token burn for multi-turn flows; second, SLOs not tied to realistic prompt sets. We recommend you provide a representative sample of long and short flows and flag any system messages. Also watch out for cold-start latency on GPUs if your traffic pattern is sporadic.
07:20 Ethan: Noted. We'll prepare the prompt set with varied lengths.
07:25 Maya: Let's talk success metrics one more time so we can lock the acceptance criteria in the SOW: p95 <200ms during the 2-hour soak at 200 QPS, error rate <0.5%, model quality delta <5% on your eval, and security docs delivered. Any objections?
07:42 Priya: Sounds good. For cost we need a model that shows per-token cost and projected monthly cost at sustained 200 QPS.
07:50 Maya: We'll provide a cost model spreadsheet that shows hosted variable pricing and a Dedicated reserved SKU estimate. We'll include sample caching and quantization scenarios to show savings.
08:05 Jared: For SSO and audit logs, can Redwood push logs to our log collector? We use Splunk.
08:12 Carlos: Yes — we support log forwarding and can push metrics or logs to your Splunk endpoint for Private and Dedicated; hosted may require a connector or log export add-on. We'll list specifics.
08:28 Priya: Ok next: acceptance test owners. Ethan will own quality eval, Jared owns infra checks, Priya will sign off overall. Maya will collate Redwood deliverables.
08:40 Maya: I'll follow up with a concrete SOW and timeline. Carlos will put the runbook and benchmark scripts in the shared folder.
08:50 Ethan: One more question — if quality doesn't meet parity, what's the fallback? Do we roll to a higher-capacity model variant?
08:58 Carlos: We can configure model fallbacks and automated routing — e.g., try quantized 13B, if quality fails, route to 34B onwards with cost-based policy. We'll demo fallback flows in the tech deep dive.
09:15 Priya: Great. Anything else?
09:18 Maya: Quick recap of next steps: pricing spreadsheet, benchmark runbook, Alder provides prompt CSV + eval set, schedule infra deep dive. We'll aim to start synthetic benchmark within 10 days.
09:30 Priya: Good. Thanks everyone.
09:34 Meeting end.

Notes on imperfect transcription: some product names may be misrecognized (Redwood Dedicated appears sometimes as Redwood "dedicate"), K-V cache transcribed as "K V cash" in places, and VPC sometimes as "V P C".
